d.title: The worked query, one stage at a time
d.caption: The row count on the right is the real count from the shop tables. Every later stage can only see what the stage above it produced — which is why `WHERE` cannot mention `n_orders` and `HAVING` can.

items.label: FROM + JOIN
items.desc: every order paired with its customer

items.label: GROUP BY  c.country
items.desc: GB, DE, NG, FR and one NULL country

items.label: HAVING  COUNT(*) >= 2
items.desc: the first stage at which the count exists

items.label: SELECT
items.desc: computes the columns and names them: n_orders is born here

items.label: ORDER BY  n_orders DESC
items.desc: runs after SELECT, so the alias resolves

items.label: LIMIT 2
items.desc: keeps the slice; meaningless without the sort above

d.title: Where an expression is allowed, and why
d.caption: Every row is the same rule read twice: a clause can only name what an earlier stage has already built. The fix is never a different syntax, it is a different clause.

d.title: Three answers, and only one of them passes the gate
d.caption: WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is **true**. Unknown and false are treated identically there, which is why a row can vanish from both `= 'GB'` and `<> 'GB'`.
cells: the only NULL test that works

d.title: What each aggregate does with a NULL
d.caption: Only `COUNT(*)` counts rows; everything else counts or sums the values that exist. The gap between `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(x)` is the number of NULLs in x — a free null check.
cells: NULL when every value is NULL
NULL is never a distinct value

d.title: The afternoon BETWEEN throws away
d.caption: `BETWEEN '2025-03-01' AND '2025-03-15'` is `>= 2025-03-01 00:00` and `<= 2025-03-15 00:00`. The right-hand string becomes midnight at the *start* of the 15th, so every order after breakfast on the 15th is outside the range. Half-open `>= start AND < next_day` is the spelling that never does this.

d.title: Three kinds of time, and what each one pins down
d.caption: The choice is about what the value *means*, not how it prints. A TIMESTAMP without a zone is a clock face with no location — two of them cannot be compared across regions without an assumption you did not write down.
cells: an event has a time of day

d.title: CASE stops at the first true branch
d.caption: The branches are tested top to bottom and the first true one wins, so an overlapping condition placed first hides every branch below it. A missing ELSE is not an error — it is a NULL.

items.label: WHEN the first condition
items.desc: tested first; if true, nothing below it runs

items.label: WHEN the second condition
items.desc: reached only when the first was false

items.label: ELSE
items.desc: the value when no branch matched

d.title: The three quiet failures, with the numbers they produce
d.caption: All three run without an error and all three are wrong. The last two are the same bug: integer division truncates, so write the `1.0` or the CAST every time and the query means the same thing on every engine.
cells: no ELSE: every row adds NULL
ELSE 0 makes it a real sum

d.title: What each number type actually promises
d.caption: FLOAT stores binary fractions, and a tenth is not one — so `0.1 + 0.2` is not `0.3` there and is in NUMERIC. Money is NUMERIC, measurements are FLOAT, and the choice is not a matter of taste.
cells: when the limit is a real rule

d.title: Why the monthly series starts in January
d.caption: A GROUP BY produces a row per period that **has** data, so November and December — which have no paid orders in the shop — are absent rather than zero, and a chart or a rolling average reads absence as a dip. `generate_series` builds the six months and a LEFT JOIN from it keeps every one, with `COALESCE` turning the empty ones into `0.00`.
